items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Earl Norman, my landlord and I had built a large table in his basement... I would borrow a few dollars from them

ctx.x: I had a few gigs now and then which were mostly then and was getting behind in my rent. But the Normans never bothered me about that and sometimes, I would borrow a few dollars from them because they knew that When I made a gig, I would pay my rent and give back the money I had borrowed. Earl Norman, my landlord and I had built a large table in his basement on which we were going to realize our dream of havin' some miniature electric trains. Earl was an automobile mechanic and a damn good one. He also knew many…

I told Norman that, and then he says that Earle Howard was the head red cap at the Pennsylvannia railroad station and asked me why didn't get a job carrying bags. He told me that in a very polite way and I told him very politely that I didn't like to carry my own bags and had no eyes for carrying those of other people. Many New York musicians had done it, but for the time being, I figured to make it in the music game, even if there was not much on the rail for the lizard.

So on November 21st of '47, I went into the 845 Club in the Bronx with a small combo lead by Billie Kyle. We were all ex-Sy Oliver members, except Charlie Holmes, the alto sax man. Freddie William was on tenor, George Duvivier on bass and Wallace Bishop on drums. The 845 Club was the only Negro night club in the Bronx
